extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, mathematical physicists, journal editors, and readers concerned with standards of rigor and publication practices
extracted.subtask_short: standards for mathematical publication and rigor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for distinguishing, labeling, validating, and crediting mathematical work (rigorous proofs, speculative/theoretical arguments, computer-assisted proofs, research announcements) and for cross-disciplinary standards with physics and computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rigorous proofs from heuristic results
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of distinguishing between results based on rigorous proofs and those which have a heuristic basis (i.e., separating proved theorems from heuristic/speculative arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple respondents echo Jaﬀe-Quinn's call to make clear what is proved versus what is heuristic. Phrases from the page: 'truth in advertising', 'clear labeling of standards which are adopted within a specific paper.' This includes explicitly flagging when statements are conjectural, heuristic, or rely on physical intuition rather than a formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit and value heuristic/speculative work in early stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow exploration of new ideas and techniques that in their creative phase may be dubious or nonrigorous; recognize their historical role in major advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive arguments note Euler, Ramanujan, Witten, and others as examples where heuristic insight preceded rigorous proof. Recommendation: accept heuristic results 'with gratitude tempered with caution' and treat them as sources of discovery rather than immediate replacements for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit allocation between conjecturers and proof authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate credit based on the relative weight of ideas vs techniques: creators of conjectures may deserve substantial credit as well as those who produce rigorous proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion cites Weil vs Deligne and Hodge as examples: posterity's credit depends on how much conception vs technique contributed. Evaluators should assess conceptual insight separately from technical execution when assigning credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of disciplinary standards for interdisciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: For work at the interface of disciplines (e.g., geometry and physics), adopt the union (not intersection) of standards from the involved fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entails that interdisciplinary papers satisfy mathematical rigor where required and scientific standards such as reproducibility, experimental confirmation, or computational verification where appropriate. Example guidance: include computer experiments, lab experiments, or field data as complementary validation when mathematical rigor is not (yet) available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear labeling / 'truth in advertising' of standards used
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should state explicitly the standards of rigor, assumptions, and whether results are claimed as proved, conjectural, or heuristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and authors should label their standards and the nature of claims. Suggested phrasing from the page includes 'clear labeling of standards which are adopted within a specific paper' and exhortations to distinguish theorems from conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and role of Research Announcements (R.A.s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research Announcements provide rapid, succinct statements of important results and are valuable to the community when accompanied by sufficient indication of method or partial writeup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments in favor: R.A.s are quicker, subject to editorial scrutiny, and help avoid premature publicizing of incomplete claims; editors should insist on seeing some writeup of proofs or evidence. R.A.s should not be suppressed but handled with responsible editorial checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and independent verification (computational/experimental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of reproducibility require that computational or experimental evidence be reproducible by others or confirmed by alternative methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in computational or applied contexts, results should be reproducible (e.g., by re-running code, using different methods, or conducting experiments). This is the analogue of experimental confirmation in the sciences and complements mathematical proof where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification and verification requirements for computer-assisted proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that rely on computer calculations must justify program correctness, numerical rounding behavior, and operating-system or runtime issues, and provide independent checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lanford and Appel–Haken examples are cited: to accept a computer-assisted proof one should (a) verify the program, (b) understand numeric rounding and system-level behavior (e.g., time-sharing), (c) provide independent verifications, and (d) document error-correction routines and checking progress. Thousands of hours of computation or microfiche listings must be accompanied by accessible verification methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date/vintage labeling and potential expiration of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach dates and vintages to published proofs; consider that acceptance might increase after a proof survives a probationary period, and belief might diminish if no independent proof appears after a long time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete suggestions include: 'carry a date', acceptance if after ten years no errors found, and an 'expiration time' (proposed thirty years) reducing confidence if no independent proof appears. Also suggested: compute a numeric validity score from label, vintage, and dependencies (controversial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify papers by rigor-status labels (Thom's threefold label)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply explicit categorical labels to papers to reflect their status of rigor/completeness: (1) crib (live mathematics), (2) tombstone cross (claiming full rigor), (3) Temple (externally certified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thom's schema: 'crib' denotes live, evolving mathematics allowing clarification; 'tombstone cross' for works claiming eternal validity; 'Temple' denotes papers certified by an external priestly body (editors/committee). Proposal includes forming a certifying body (e.g., IMU-appointed) for bestowing 'Temple' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature publicity of unproven claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not widely publicize alleged proofs without providing details in print or refereed form; announcing results with publicity but without proofs is inexcusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labelled 'Don't Prove, Just Lecture!': lectures or press publicity about claimed solutions without published, refereed proofs waste time and mislead. Variants include publishing in unrefereed venues without detail; such practices should be discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and completeness for large-scale collaborative proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, distributed proofs (e.g., classification of finite simple groups) must be transparent about completeness and the status of outsourced or unfinished parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts were farmed out or remain incomplete, the mathematical community should be informed; there should be clarity about who has verified which parts and where gaps remain, because long multi-author projects are likely to contain mistakes and need organized verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in relying on symbolic/numerical packages (Mathematica, Maple)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about relying on large symbolic/numeric software as a basis for proofs; verify outputs and be aware of possible software or data errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples note that Maple output once produced an apparent counterexample to unique factorization—showing the need to verify and not blindly trust CAS outputs. Proofs relying on such systems may require extra labeling or verification to be considered fully rigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for awarding credit to proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit for producing proofs should reflect factors such as whether the proof disconfirms theoretical ideas, the difficulty of the proof, originality of methods, and the fruitfulness of the ideas involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friedan and others suggest proofs receive significant credit when they overturn theory, are especially difficult, or introduce original, fruitful ideas; pedestrian proofs might receive less recognition. There is skepticism about formalizing rigid credit rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical obligation to understand results one uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers have an ethical responsibility not to use results whose proofs they do not understand (except when aiming to disprove them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thom argues it is unethical to use a result whose proof one does not comprehend; this presumes 'understanding' means thorough knowledge of all arguments. Practical exceptions exist, but caution is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as narrative and use of assumptions to suggest experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may present mathematics with assumed hypotheses or speculative steps to create a persuasive narrative whose role is to suggest experiments or computational checks rather than immediate theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: authors introduce assumptions like 'assume series converges' or 'assume equilibrium is stable' to tell a coherent story; validation is expected from experiments or computations, and such narrative mathematics can be indispensable in applied contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology precision: prefer 'speculative mathematics' to 'theoretical mathematics'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid coining or adopting misleading terminology; 'theoretical mathematics' (as used by Jaﬀe-Quinn) is contested and may better be called 'speculative mathematics'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics note that 'theory' has established meanings in mathematics; adopting 'theoretical' for speculative work risks confusion. Use precise labels to avoid conflating different meanings of 'theory'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize mathematics' self-correcting nature and evolving standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of rigor are relative, sociological, and evolve over time; the community's self-correcting mechanisms eventually resolve many earlier gaps or sloppy arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Poincaré, Cartan, Italian algebraic geometry, etc.) show that apparent lapses were later resolved. Policies should respect freedom for diverse methods while maintaining incentives toward rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label proofs by method (computer-aided, mass collaboration, formal, informal, constructive, fuzzy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach methodological labels to proofs indicating how the proof was obtained (e.g., computer-aided, mass collaboration, formal proof-assistant, informal/heuristic, constructive, fuzzy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such labels help readers assess reliability; suggested labels include computer-aided, mass collaboration, formal, informal, constructive, fuzzy. These labels can be inputs to a (controversial) numeric validity measure or used simply for reader guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and referee responsibility for critical scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and referees must actively scrutinize claims, insist on sufficient writeups for R.A.s, and guard against network endorsement leading to uncritical acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that 'theoretical mathematics' claims can be reinforced by networks of endorsing experts; editors/referees should ensure claims are properly vetted and that research announcements include evidence of the underlying proof or methods.
